throat noun

also gullet, my throat hurts, clear one’s throat, a lump in one’s throat, esophagus

classical

Plin. NH 11.179: summum gulae faucēs vocantur (Lewis & Short)
Quint. 11.3.20: faucēs tumentēs (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 56, 393
Traupman 59
Traupman 66

faucēs, faucium f. pl.

noun, third declension, plural

throat, the back of the mouth

The everyday word for the throat as it gets sore, dry or hoarse; plural in prose (the singular fauce is poetic). Also the narrow entrance of anything, a pass or a gorge (see gorge).

Other words

  • guttur, gutturis n. — throat, gullet

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Ov. Am. 1.13.8: liquidum tenuī gutture cantat avis (Lewis & Short); Juv. 13.162

    The gullet and the throat from outside, as a bird sings with it or a goitre swells in it; also, by transfer, gluttony (Juv. 2.114). Lewis & Short marks it chiefly ante-classical and poetic.

  • gula, gulae f. — gullet

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Plin. NH 11.179 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 58; Traupman 310

    The gullet, the passage food goes down; much more often greed for food (gulae parēre, Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • caret ōs ūmōre loquentis et faucēs ārent, vixque est via vōcis in illīs

    my mouth is dry as I speak, my throat is parched, and there is hardly a way through it for my voiceOv. Met. 6.354–355

  • obstipuī, steteruntque comae et vōx faucibus haesit

    I froze, my hair stood on end and my voice stuck in my throatVerg. A. 2.774

See also sore throat, neck, gorge.
